story: In September 2024, Herbert Kickl's Freedom Party won an Austrian national election for the first time since its founding by former Nazis in the 1950s. Every other party had promised not to govern with him. Austria then spent five months proving how hard keeping that promise would be: centrist coalition talks collapsed, the conservatives briefly negotiated with Kickl, and those talks collapsed too. In March 2025, Christian Stocker, a little-known conservative who became chancellor almost by accident, formed a three-party coalition of the centre-right ÖVP, the Social Democrats and the liberal NEOS whose main shared purpose was keeping Kickl out (CIDOB).

2026 showed the cost of that bargain. To close a large budget deficit in a recession-hit economy tied to Germany's, the coalition passed an unpopular austerity package, and voters blamed it. By summer, polls had the FPÖ at around 34 percent and Stocker's ÖVP at 18 to 19; asked whom they would pick directly as chancellor, only 8 percent chose Stocker and 29 percent chose Kickl (Börse Express). Stocker went on a summer tour of the country trying to reconnect, while a business-chamber scandal in Vienna gave Kickl fresh material. Commentators argued Stocker's best hope was to make himself the anti-Trump candidate, since Kickl openly admires Trump and Viktor Orbán (Vol.at). That bet looked better after Orbán himself lost power in Hungary in April. The question hanging over Austria is whether a coalition built to block one man can govern well enough to stop him winning outright next time.
briefing.power: A federal parliamentary republic. The chancellor leads the government with the support of the 183-seat National Council, elected by proportional representation; the directly elected federal president, Alexander Van der Bellen, appoints the chancellor and can refuse to.
briefing.holders: Chancellor Christian Stocker (ÖVP), in a coalition with the SPÖ and NEOS.
